paras: The attacks on Black miners at Virginia City, Alabama, were a series of shootings and beatings in August 1903 at a coal-mining camp in Jefferson County, where union miners were on strike. Striking miners were reported to have fired into the Black quarters at the mines on two nights, to have threatened a Black guard with lynching and shot him, and days later to have shot one Black man and beaten another on the road. No one was reported killed, and charges against three white men were dropped within two weeks.

Virginia City was a mining camp in the southern part of Jefferson County, near Birmingham and Bessemer, where members of the United Mine Workers of America had been on strike for some time. According to the Tribune's Birmingham correspondent, the mine company had repeatedly had strikers arrested, but the court had discharged them every time. The mines were operated by the Schulers, who were also described as building a stockade at Gadsden to hold convicts for work on a furnace and steel mill. A wire report said the trouble came from an effort to work non-union men in the mines.

The New-York Tribune's correspondent reported, as an allegation, that the strikers surrounded the "negro quarters" at the mines on the nights of August 8 and 9 and fired one volley into the houses each night, wounding one man on the second night. A Black man who had been on guard duty said that the miners captured him and took him into the woods, where he was threatened with lynching. He was then allowed to go back to the camp but was shot at and wounded on the way. On August 10 a report reached Sheriff Burgin of serious trouble and some shooting, one man shot and another assaulted, and he sent a posse of deputies, twenty-five according to the Tribune.

Violence resumed on the night of August 12, when Joe Williams, a Black man, was shot and seriously wounded about a mile from Virginia City and Earnest Griffin, also Black, was beaten into insensibility. The Montgomery Advertiser placed the attack on the road from Virginia City to Bessemer and said those responsible were not known, while the Tribune reported that a white woman was said to have been among the assailants and that the miners were heavily armed. More deputies went to the camp on August 13.

Two white men were arrested and charged with assault with intent to murder and highway robbery, and a force of deputies was to remain at the mines for several days. On August 22 the Advertiser reported that cases against Lil and Rufe Morrison and Frank Jones, white, charged on complaints by Black men with assault with intent to murder and robbery arising from the Virginia City disturbances, had been nol prossed in Justice Tillman's court in Bessemer. The same item noted that the union miners were still on strike. No report of charges over the earlier volleys or the attack on the guard appears in the coverage.

Only the New-York Tribune, through its own Birmingham telegrams, presented the episode as racial violence, under the headlines "Miners Shoot at Negroes" and "Renew Attacks on Negroes," the second subtitled "White Woman in Mob That Shoots Black Miners." Even so, it qualified its first account with "it is alleged" and relayed the lynching threat in the guard's own words.

The Birmingham wire that ran in the Savannah Morning News, the Bisbee Daily Review and the Salt Lake Herald on August 11 treated the events as a labor dispute, "Alabama Strike Riot," naming no race and attributing the trouble to the hiring of non-union men. The Montgomery Advertiser's Birmingham reports likewise centered the sheriff and the strike, though it later gave the names and race of the August 12 victims and briefly recorded the arrests and the dropped charges. By August 20 the story had shrunk to a single digest line in the Berea, Kentucky, Citizen, and no Black-press account appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Attacks on Black miners at Virginia City, Alabama
bases: Striking miners were reported to have surrounded the Black quarters at the mines on two nights and fired into the houses, then to have attacked individual Black men on the roads, in the course of a coal strike (A1, A3, A6, A7).

The Tribune's own Birmingham correspondent and the separate Associated Press-style wire both report shooting and an assault at the Virginia City strike on Aug. 9-10 (A1, A2, A4), and the Aug. 12 shooting and beating is reported by both the Tribune and the Montgomery Advertiser (A6, A7, A8); only the Tribune names the Black quarters and the lynching threat (A1).

accounts.label: Tribune Birmingham correspondent
accounts.gist: Striking miners were 'alleged' to have surrounded the negro quarters two nights and fired into the houses, wounding one man; a Black guard said miners threatened to lynch him and shot him. A second dispatch reported a mob, including a white woman, shooting and beating Black miners.

accounts.label: Birmingham wire (sheriff's report)
accounts.gist: A report to the sheriff told of serious trouble and some shooting at the strike, one man shot and another assaulted, said to arise from an effort to work non-union men; race not stated.

accounts.label: Montgomery Advertiser Birmingham reports
accounts.gist: Named Joe Williams and Earnest Griffin as the Black men shot and beaten on Aug. 12, said the attackers were unknown, then reported two white men arrested and, a week later, charges against three white men dropped.

framing.detail: The New-York Tribune headlined 'MINERS SHOOT AT NEGROES' and 'RENEW ATTACKS ON NEGROES', naming the targets' race and a 'White Woman in Mob', while hedging the first account as 'alleged'.
The Birmingham wire ran as a labor story, 'Alabama Strike Riot' and 'Strike at Virginia City', blaming an effort to work non-union men and naming no race.
The Montgomery Advertiser's headlines ('Burgin Sends Posse', 'Trouble at Mines', 'Virginia City Troubles') centered the sheriff and the strike, and it reported the dropped charges in a brief item.
